741.quote_or_event: “Erect a wall, gates, and battlements; dig a moat; construct śataghnîs: then you will be a Kshattriya.”
741.explanation: In the Uttaradhyayana's dialogue on King Nami's renunciation, Indra, disguised as a Brahmin, urges the departing king that fortifying his city is the very mark of a warrior-ruler; Nami answers that the only fortress worth building is an inner one.
741.tie_back: Indra's advice voices exactly the Kural's premise that a fort is the prized possession of a king, while the Jain text then turns that premise toward renunciation.
741.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
741._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); the verse states the Kural's view of the fort as a king's essential asset, but the Jain text puts it in the mouth of the tempter and does not endorse it, so the fit is partial.

742.quote_or_event: “At each gate they made a tank with golden lotuses having four gates like the rampart of the samavasaraṇa.” … “In the midst of the samavasaraṇa, a caitya-tree made by the Vyantaras, rising for three kos, indicated the rise of the Three Jewels.”
742.explanation: Hemacandra's description of the samavasarana, the assembly hall the gods raise for a Tirthankara's preaching, sets pools of water at its gates and a great shade-giving sacred tree at its centre within its ramparts.
742.tie_back: The Jain sacred enclosure combines clear water and a towering tree inside its walls, a distant echo of the Kural's natural defences of gem-clear water, open ground, hill and shady forest, though its purpose is sermon and refuge, not war.
742.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra 1.3, part 10 ‘Description of a samavasaraṇa’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931; wisdomlib.org)
742._accuracy_note: Both sentences verified verbatim against Johnson's translation on wisdomlib.org; Jain scripture has no teaching on the natural defences of a fort, so this is a next-best structural echo only (no hill or forest belt is described).

743.quote_or_event: “It may be noted that three gunavratas and four siksavratas are grouped together and are known as silavratas, i.e., supplementary vows because these vows perform the work of supplementing or protecting the five main anuvratas just as towns are protected or guarded by the encircling walls built around them.”
743.explanation: Jain householder ethics treats the seven supplementary vows as a protective wall thrown around the five small vows of non-violence, truth, non-stealing, chastity and non-possession.
743.tie_back: Where the Kural specifies the height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility of a town's wall, Jainism borrows the same image of the encircling wall to explain how the supplementary vows guard the core vows.
743.source: Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’, section on the twelve vratas (jainworld.com)
743._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the jainworld.com page; this is a secondary scholar's summary of the traditional simile, and it uses the town wall as a metaphor without listing its qualities, so the match is partial.

744.quote_or_event: “Anativyakte gupte sthane suprativesmike aneka- nirgamadvaravivarjita-niketana : Dwelling in a place which is not too exposed and not too enclosed, with good neighbors, and few exits.”
744.explanation: Among Hemacandra's thirty-five qualities of an ideal Jain householder is living in a well-sited home that is neither too exposed nor too shut in and has only a few ways in and out, the traditional reasoning being security against thieves.
744.tie_back: The Kural's fort with few points to guard and ample room inside is matched, on a domestic scale, by the Jain householder's dwelling with few exits that is neither too open nor too cramped.
744.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, no. 7, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, ‘Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code’ (jainworld.com)
744._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (including the source's hyphen spacing) on jainworld.com; the design principle of few exits is a genuine parallel, but it concerns a layman's house, not a royal fort, and says nothing about breaking an attacker's spirit.

745.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable …”
745.explanation: Nami replies to Indra that a sage's true fortress is built from faith, austerity, self-control and patience, and that, guarded by the three guptis of mind, speech and body, it cannot be taken.
745.tie_back: The Kural asks for a fortress that is hard to capture and easy to hold; the Jain sage describes an inner citadel that is impregnable because its gate is barred by self-control and its wall is patience.
745.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.20–22, first half (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
745._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (quotation stops mid-sentence at the ellipsis); the impregnability theme fits strongly, but the Jain fortress is spiritual and the Kural's stress on stored provisions has no counterpart.

746.quote_or_event: “On both sides of the east gate of the first rampart stood two gold-colored Vaimānika-gods as door-keepers.” … “At the four gates of the second wall, in the same order beginning with the east, stood the goddesses Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā and Aparājitā, all having one hand in the position bestowing fearlessness …”
746.explanation: In Hemacandra's account of Rishabha's assembly hall, every gate of every rampart is held by divine guardians, and the goddesses at the second wall raise the hand that grants fearlessness to those within.
746.tie_back: The Kural's fort is complete only when it has good and valiant defenders to help in danger, and the Jain samavasarana likewise stations guardians at each gate who give security to all inside.
746.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra 1.3, part 10 ‘Description of a samavasaraṇa’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS, 1931; wisdomlib.org)
746._accuracy_note: Both sentences verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; the guardians are celestial door-keepers of a peaceful preaching hall rather than soldiers of a garrison, so this is an imagistic next-best match.

747.quote_or_event: “Though others sleep, be thou awake! Like a wise man, trust nobody, but be always on the alert; for dangerous is the time and weak the body.”
747.explanation: Mahavira's sermon on carelessness tells the monk to keep constant watch and not rely on anyone, because danger can come at any moment and the body is frail.
747.tie_back: The Kural's fortress must withstand siege, assault and betrayal from within; the Jain call to stay awake and trust nobody is the same vigilance against an enemy who strikes when the guard is down, applied to the soul.
747.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
747._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the warning against trusting others touches the Kural's concern with treachery, but the verse is about spiritual vigilance and does not address military siege.

748.quote_or_event: “… making Zeal his bow, its string Carefulness in walking (iriyâ), and its top (where the string is fastened) Content, he should bend (this bow) with Truth, piercing with the arrow, Penance, (the foe's) mail, Karman--(in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Saṃsâra.”
748.explanation: Continuing his reply to Indra, Nami says that the sage, defending from within his fortress of faith, fights back with the bow of zeal and the arrow of penance and pierces the armour of karma.
748.tie_back: As the Kural's defenders, holding their ground, defeat even an expert besieging army, the Jain sage holds his inner fortress and from it overcomes the besieging force of karma.
748.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.20–22, second half (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
748._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritic on Saṃsâra normalised); the image of defenders winning from within the fort fits well, but the enemy is karma, not an army, and siegecraft is not described.

749.quote_or_event: “Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself.”
749.explanation: Nami answers Indra's call to subdue rival princes by ranking self-conquest above any number of battlefield victories.
749.tie_back: The Kural praises a fort whose defenders win renown by felling the enemy at the battle-front; Jainism accepts that such victories happen but holds that the more glorious victory is won over oneself.
749.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
749._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shares the Kural's language of victory in battle but deliberately relativises martial glory, which Jain ahimsa does not celebrate, so it is a partial, contrasting match.

750.quote_or_event: “You cannot prolong your life, therefore be not careless; you are past help when old age approaches. Consider this: what (protection) will careless people get, who kill living beings and do not exert themselves?”
750.explanation: The fourth lecture of the Uttaradhyayana warns that nothing can protect those who are careless and do not exert themselves; protection depends on one's own vigilant effort.
750.tie_back: The Kural ends by saying even the finest fortress is no fortress for those who lack skill and vigour in action, and the Jain verse likewise denies any protection to people who will not exert themselves.
750.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
750._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the shared point that protection fails without exertion is real, but the Jain verse concerns spiritual carelessness and death, not defending a fort.
